title: The Contract Is the Beginning
description: The signature closes a negotiation. It also begins the relationship that determines whether the agreement succeeds.
body: A signed contract can feel like the finish line. After months of discussion, negotiation and revision, the document is finally complete.
But in my experience, the signature is not the end of the work. It is the beginning of a different kind of work.

Customers rarely remember every clause that was negotiated. They remember whether working with you made their job easier. They remember whether you returned the difficult call, stayed close when something went wrong, and followed through when no one was watching.

The strongest commercial relationships are built after the excitement of winning has passed. They are built through delivery, consistency and the quiet confidence that someone has one less thing to worry about because you are involved.
A contract records the agreement. Trust determines what that agreement becomes.

title: Beyond Networking
description: Some of the strongest relationships are built while doing meaningful work together—not while exchanging introductions.
body: I have never been particularly comfortable with the word networking. It can make relationships sound like something collected rather than something built.

The relationships that have mattered most in my life rarely began with an agenda. They began with shared work: solving a problem, building a project, helping a classmate or showing up repeatedly for a community.

Working across teams at UCLA reinforced something I had experienced throughout my career. Collaboration reveals people in ways introductions cannot. You learn how someone listens, how they respond when plans change, whether they share credit and whether they can be relied upon.
Perhaps the better question is not, ‘How many people did I meet?’ It is, ‘What did we build together?’

title: Two Dogs After Forty Years
description: I spent most of my life without a dog. Percy and Pluto quietly changed what I notice about presence, patience and home.
body: For more than forty years, I never had a dog. Then Percy and Pluto entered our lives, and routines I had never considered important suddenly became part of each day.
They do not understand calendars, job titles or unfinished emails. They understand whether you are present. They notice your return, your tone and the small rituals that tell them they belong.

Living with them has made patience less abstract. It has made consistency visible. Trust is built through the same walk, the same bowl, the same return home—ordinary actions repeated until they become certainty.
They changed our house, but more importantly, they changed what I notice inside it.
